pos: n. (the Hessian abbey founded in 744 where Boniface is buried, whose library preserved the Latin Diatessaron and whose scriptorium taught Germany to write)
etymology: From the river Fulda, an Old High German name of uncertain sense.
biblical_def: Fulda was founded in 744 by Sturm at the direction of Boniface, and when Boniface was killed in Frisia ten years later his body was brought here, which made the abbey the chief religious centre of Germany. Under Hrabanus Maurus, abbot from 822 and the most learned man in the Frankish world, its school and scriptorium produced commentaries, a Latin encyclopaedia, the first German-Latin glossaries and a body of copying that transmitted much of what survives of Latin literature; its library held the codex of the Latin gospel harmony prefaced by Victor of Capua, which is still called the Fulda codex. The abbot became a prince of the Empire. Fulda remained Catholic through the Reformation, received a Jesuit college in 1571, and was one of the centres from which the Catholic Reformation worked in central Germany. The dictionary records Fulda for the scriptorium. The transmission of texts by hand, generation after generation, by men who did not write them and were not famous, is the mechanism by which the church has what it has.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a scriptorium is not in Webster, but a scribe is one who writes or copies; transmission as the act of sending from one to another; a library as a collection of books; a copy as a transcript; and tradition as the delivery of things from hand to hand.
webster_full: SCRIBE, n. A writer; a notary; one who writes or copies; in the Jewish nation, a clerk or secretary to the king, and a doctor of the law.
TRANSMISSION, n. The act of sending from one place or person to another; the sending or conveying of a thing from one person to another.
LIBRARY, n. A collection of books belonging to a private person, or to a public institution or a company.
COPY, n. A transcript from an original; a writing like another writing; an imitation or likeness.
TRADITION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices, rites and customs from father to son, or from ancestors to posterity.
scriptures: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the LORD.
Take this book of the law, and put it in the side of the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God, that it may be there for a witness against thee.
Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah hath burned.
corruption_summary: Hessian abbey of 744 where Boniface is buried, whose scriptorium under Hrabanus Maurus transmitted much of Latin literature and preserved the Fulda gospel harmony.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour of transmission. Scripture treats the handing on of the deposit as a command with a chain of custody built into it: “And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2). A copyist in a Hessian cloister is a link in that chain whether he knows it or not.

The second paragraph names the live temptation, which is to despise the unglamorous work that keeps a text alive. Scripture does the opposite. The psalmist expects his words to reach a generation not yet born, “This shall be written for the generation to come” (Psa 102:18); Moses commands the book to be put in a place where it will be kept, “Take this book of the law, and put it in the side of the ark of the covenant” (Deu 31:26); and when a king burns a scroll the answer is to write it again, “Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words” (Jer 36:28). Fulda's monks did that for four centuries, and nobody knows most of their names.

Hebrew kathab (H3789) — to write, to inscribe; “This shall be written for the generation to come”, Psalm 102:18.
Hebrew sepher (H5612) — a book, a writing, a scroll; “Take this book of the law”, Deuteronomy 31:26.
Hebrew megillah (H4039) — a roll, a scroll; “Take thee again another roll”, Jeremiah 36:28.

“This shall be written for the generation to come” (Psa 102:18) — why copying is not a trivial trade.
“Take thee again another roll” (Jer 36:28) — the answer when a king burns a scroll.

pos: n. (the Franconian prince-bishopric of Kilian's mission and of the witch trials of 1626 to 1631, in which some nine hundred people were burned)
etymology: From Old High German wirz, a herb or plant, and burg, a fortress.
biblical_def: Wurzburg on the Main was evangelised by the Irish missionary Kilian, killed about 689, and made a see by Boniface in 742; its bishops were also dukes of Franconia and ruled a substantial territory from the Marienberg fortress. The town was a centre of the Catholic Reformation under Julius Echter von Mespelbrunn, who founded the university in 1582, expelled Protestants and built or restored hundreds of churches. Under his successor Philipp Adolf von Ehrenberg, between 1626 and 1631, the prince-bishopric conducted one of the largest witch persecutions in European history: something near nine hundred people were executed, including children, priests, the bishop's own nephew, and the chancellor of the university, on evidence obtained by torture. The neighbouring see of Bamberg did the same. The dictionary records Wurzburg because the witch trials are the clearest case in church history of a judicial machine manufacturing the crime it punished, and because the men who stopped it argued from Scripture.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines witchcraft as the practices of witches; torture as extreme pain inflicted judicially; a confession as an acknowledgment of a crime; evidence as that which makes clear; and credulity as easiness of belief.
webster_full: WITCHCRAFT, n. The practices of witches; sorcery; enchantments; intercourse with the devil; power more than natural.
TORTURE, n. Extreme pain; anguish of body or mind; severe pain inflicted judicially, either as a punishment or for the purpose of extorting confessions.
CONFESSION, n. The acknowledgment of a crime, fault or something that is disadvantageous to one's own interest.
EVIDENCE, n. That which elucidates and enables the mind to see truth; proof arising from the testimony of others.
CREDULITY, n. Easiness of belief; a disposition or readiness to believe without sufficient evidence.
scriptures: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sinneth: at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established.
He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
And the judges shall make diligent inquisition: and, behold, if the witness be a false witness, and hath testified falsely against his brother;
Exo 23:7
Keep thee far from a false matter; and the innocent and righteous slay thou not: for I will not justify the wicked.
corruption_summary: Franconian prince-bishopric where some nine hundred people, including children and clergy, were burned as witches between 1626 and 1631 on evidence obtained by torture.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the judicial machine that produces its own evidence. Torture makes a confession available on demand, and once the accused is required to name accomplices the process is self-feeding, which is exactly what happened at Wurzburg and Bamberg, where the accused eventually included the men running the courts. Scripture closes the mechanism with a rule about witnesses that the trials abolished: “at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” (Deu 19:15).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. The accuser must himself be examined, “And the judges shall make diligent inquisition” (Deu 19:18); the opposing party must be heard, since “He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him” (Pro 18:17); and the law forbids the conviction of the innocent in a form that gives the judge no escape: “the innocent and righteous slay thou not: for I will not justify the wicked” (Exo 23:7). The dictionary adds that the Jesuit Friedrich Spee, who had attended the condemned, published in 1631 the argument that broke the trials in Germany, and that it was an argument about procedure and evidence and not about whether witchcraft exists.

pos: n. (the Franconian see founded in 1007 whose witch trials of 1626 to 1631 killed about a thousand people in a purpose-built prison)
etymology: From Old High German Babenberg, the hill of Babo, a personal name.
biblical_def: Bamberg was founded as a see in 1007 by the emperor Henry the Second, who is buried in its cathedral with his wife Kunigunde, and became a prince-bishopric on the Regnitz with a great Romanesque cathedral and later a baroque city. Under Prince-Bishop Johann Georg the Second Fuchs von Dornheim, from 1623, it ran a witch persecution comparable to Wurzburg's: about a thousand people were executed between 1626 and 1631, a purpose-built interrogation house called the Drudenhaus was erected, and the accused included five successive burgomasters of the city, with their property confiscated to the bishop's treasury. The emperor Ferdinand the Second intervened against the trials in 1630 and 1631, and the Swedish advance ended them. The dictionary records Bamberg beside Wurzburg because the detail that explains both is the confiscation. Where a conviction enriches the court that convicts, the court will convict, and no amount of theology about the devil is required to account for a thousand deaths.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines confiscation as the adjudging of forfeited property to the state; a burgomaster as the chief magistrate of a Dutch or German town; interrogation as the act of questioning; covetousness as an inordinate desire of gain; and bribery as the act of giving a reward to pervert judgment.
webster_full: CONFISCATION, n. The act of condemning as forfeited, and adjudging to the public treasury; the seizure of private property by government.
BURGOMASTER, n. A burgess; a magistrate; the chief magistrate of a municipal town in Holland, Flanders and Germany.
INTERROGATION, n. The act of questioning; examination by questions; a question put.
COVETOUSNESS, n. A strong or inordinate desire of obtaining and possessing some supposed good; avarice.
BRIBERY, n. The act or practice of giving or taking rewards for corrupt practices; the act of paying for official misconduct.
scriptures: Exo 23:8
And thou shalt take no gift: for the gift blindeth the wise, and perverteth the words of the righteous.

And thou shalt speak unto him, saying, Thus saith the LORD, Hast thou killed, and also taken possession? And thou shalt speak unto him, saying, Thus saith the LORD, In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick thy blood, even thine.
For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
Mic 3:11

The heads thereof judge for reward, and the priests thereof teach for hire, and the prophets thereof divine for money: yet will they lean upon the LORD, and say, Is not the LORD among us? none evil can come upon us.
corruption_summary: Franconian see whose witch trials killed about a thousand people between 1626 and 1631, with the property of the condemned confiscated to the bishop's treasury.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is a court that profits by its own verdicts, which is bribery with the stages reversed: instead of a litigant paying the judge, the conviction pays him. The law forbids the ordinary form and gives the reason in terms of what money does to sight: “And thou shalt take no gift: for the gift blindeth the wise, and perverteth the words of the righteous” (Exo 23:8). Micah describes a whole establishment working this way, where “the priests thereof teach for hire, and the prophets thereof divine for money” (Mic 3:11).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. The sentence on a ruler who killed a man to take his land is the plainest word in Scripture for what Bamberg did, and the prophet was sent to say it to his face: “Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?” (1Ki 21:19). Paul supplies the diagnosis that covers the bishop, the judges and the informers together: “For the love of money is the root of all evil” (1Ti 6:10). The dictionary holds that the theological debate about witchcraft, real as it was, is not the explanation of these trials. The explanation is in the ledgers.

“For the love of money is the root of all evil” (1Ti 6:10) — the diagnosis that covers all parties.

pos: n. (the Bavarian see at the meeting of three rivers where the treaty of 1552 granted Lutherans a provisional peace before Augsburg)
etymology: From Latin Batavis, a Roman fort of the Batavian cohort, through Old High German Pazzowa.
biblical_def: Passau stands where the Ilz and the Inn meet the Danube on the Austrian border, a Roman fort, a see from 739, and for centuries the largest diocese in the Empire, with jurisdiction reaching down the Danube to Vienna. Its name belongs to a treaty. After Maurice of Saxony's revolt had defeated Charles the Fifth's attempt to impose the Augsburg Interim by force, the treaty of Passau was signed on the second of August 1552: it released Philip of Hesse and John Frederick of Saxony from imprisonment, suspended the Interim, and granted the Lutheran estates liberty of religion until a general settlement. That settlement came three years later as the Peace of Augsburg. The dictionary records Passau as the point at which the Empire conceded that Lutheranism could not be suppressed by arms, and notes what the concession actually was: not liberty of conscience for persons, but liberty for estates, with each prince deciding for his own territory.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an interim as the meantime or intervening time; an estate as a rank or class in a legislature; a truce as a temporary cessation of hostilities; a concession as the act of yielding; and conscience as the internal judge of right and wrong.
webster_full: INTERIM, n. The meantime; the intervening time; as in the interim, in the meantime.
ESTATE, n. In a political sense, a rank or class of men in the community, as the three estates of the realm.
TRUCE, n. A temporary cessation of hostilities, by agreement of the parties; an armistice.
CONCESSION, n. The act of granting or yielding; usually implying a demand, claim or request from the party to whom it is made.
CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; the faculty which decides on the lawfulness of our own actions.
scriptures: Rom 14:5
One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.
So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
corruption_summary: Bavarian see where the treaty of 1552 suspended the Augsburg Interim and granted the Lutheran estates liberty of religion until the Peace of Augsburg in 1555.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the assumption, built into the Passau and Augsburg settlements alike, that a prince's conscience can stand in for his subjects'. The dictionary grants that the treaty was better than the war it ended, and insists that what it granted was territorial and not personal. Paul puts conviction in religion where no treaty can put it, in the individual before God: “Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind” (Rom 14:5), and he gives the reason, that each will answer for himself: “So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God” (Rom 14:12).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. Where a magistrate commands what God forbids the subject's duty is settled and is not a matter for negotiation, “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29); and where he does not, the believer owes him and his neighbours the most peaceable life he can manage, “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men” (Rom 12:18). The dictionary holds that the Reformation's political settlements were a mercy and not a doctrine, and that the men who later argued for liberty of conscience as a personal right were building on the New Testament rather than on Passau.

pos: n. (the Bavarian city of the 1541 colloquy at which Contarini and Melanchthon nearly agreed a doctrine of justification, and seat of the perpetual Imperial Diet)
etymology: From Latin Castra Regina, the camp on the Regen, through Old High German Reganesburg.
biblical_def: Regensburg on the Danube was a Roman legionary camp, a free imperial city, and from 1663 to 1806 the permanent seat of the Imperial Diet. The city itself adopted the Lutheran Reformation in 1542 while remaining the meeting place of a Catholic empire. Its most important moment was the colloquy of 1541, held at the Diet, where Johann Gropper and Julius Pflug for the Catholic side and Melanchthon, Bucer and Pistorius for the Protestant worked through the Regensburg Book with the papal legate Gasparo Contarini present; they reached a formula on justification by faith, with an imputed and an inherent righteousness distinguished, which both Luther and Rome rejected, and the colloquy failed on the mass, on the church and on the authority of councils. The dictionary records Regensburg as the nearest the sixteenth century came to an agreed doctrine of justification, and as the proof that the division was not a misunderstanding. Men of real goodwill with full command of the texts could not make the formula hold.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a colloquy as a conference or conversation; imputation as the attributing of something to a person; inherent as existing in something; a formula as a prescribed form of words; and a diet as an assembly of states.
webster_full: COLLOQUY, n. Conversation; mutual discourse of two or more; a conference; a dialogue.
IMPUTATION, n. The act of imputing or charging; attribution; the reckoning to a person of something not his own by act.
INHERENT, a. Naturally pertaining to; existing in something so as to be inseparable from it; innate.
FORMULA, n. A prescribed form; a rule or model; in theology, a confession of faith reduced to set words.
DIET, n. An assembly of princes or delegates for legislative or other political purposes; a convention.
scriptures: Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
Rom 4:5
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.
Gal 2:16

Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.
Php 3:9
And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:
corruption_summary: Bavarian city of the 1541 colloquy where Contarini and Melanchthon agreed a double formula on justification that both Luther and Rome rejected.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the double justification formula itself, and the dictionary names it carefully because the men who drafted it were serious and because its modern descendants are everywhere. The Regensburg Book allowed a righteousness imputed to the believer and a righteousness inherent in him, and said that the second as well as the first has a part in his acceptance. That second clause is the whole question, and Paul excludes it: the man who is justified is described as one “that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly” (Rom 4:5).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. Justification is a verdict grounded wholly outside the man who receives it, which is why Paul can state it as a conclusion that bars contribution, “a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28), and repeat the exclusion for emphasis, “by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified” (Gal 2:16). His own account of what he wants to be found in sets the two kinds of righteousness against each other rather than adding them: “not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ” (Php 3:9). Contarini went home and died within the year, and the formula died with him.

pos: n. (the Austrian archbishopric whose archbishop expelled some twenty thousand Protestants in 1731 and 1732, many of whom settled in Georgia)
etymology: From Old High German salz, salt, and burg, a fortress, for the salt trade of the Salzach.
biblical_def: Salzburg was a Roman town, a see from 739 under Rupert and Virgil, and from the fourteenth century an independent archbishopric whose prince-archbishops ruled a mountain state until 1803. Protestantism survived in its Alpine valleys, especially the Defereggen and the Pongau, among miners and farmers who kept Lutheran books for two centuries. In 1731 Archbishop Leopold Anton von Firmian issued an edict of emigration; in the winter of 1731 and the spring of 1732 some twenty thousand people were expelled, many given only days to leave and forced to sell their holdings at a loss, and children under twelve were retained to be raised Catholic. Frederick William the First of Prussia settled most of them in East Prussia; one party reached the new colony of Georgia in 1734 and founded Ebenezer on the Savannah. The dictionary records the Salzburg expulsion as the last mass religious expulsion in western Europe, and as the plainest instance of a confessing people kept by Scripture alone, with no minister, for two hundred years.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines emigration as the removal from one country to another; an edict as a public ordinance; a refugee as one who flees for safety; a colony as a body of settlers; and perseverance as continuance in a state of grace.
webster_full: EMIGRATION, n. The act of removing from one country or state to another, for the purpose of residence.
EDICT, n. That which is uttered or proclaimed by authority as a rule of action; an order or ordinance by authority.
REFUGEE, n. One who flies to a shelter or place of safety; one who, in times of persecution or political commotion, flees to a foreign country for safety.
COLONY, n. A company of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country.
PERSEVERANCE, n. Persistence in any thing undertaken; in theology, continuance in a state of grace to a state of glory.
scriptures: These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
Thy statutes have been my songs in the house of my pilgrimage.
But when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another: for verily I say unto you, Ye shall not have gone over the cities of Israel, till the Son of man be come.
But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city.
corruption_summary: Austrian archbishopric whose 1731 edict expelled some twenty thousand Protestants from its Alpine valleys, many settling in East Prussia and in Georgia.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the expulsion of a population for its religion, carried out in 1731 by a Christian prelate against people who had committed no crime but possession of Lutheran books. Children under twelve were kept back. The dictionary names it as theft and kidnapping with an episcopal signature, and sets beside it the description Hebrews gives of such people, who die without receiving what was promised and are commended for it: they “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that a people may be kept by the word alone. These valleys had no pastors for generations and kept the faith by reading, by households and by memory, which is the psalmist's own account of how a man survives displacement: “Thy statutes have been my songs in the house of my pilgrimage” (Psa 119:54). Christ licenses the flight itself, “But when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another” (Mat 10:23), and Hebrews names what the exiles were actually looking for, “a better country, that is, an heavenly” (Heb 11:16). Some of them found a river in Georgia and called the place Ebenezer, which is a stone of help.

“Thy statutes have been my songs in the house of my pilgrimage” (Psa 119:54) — how valleys without pastors kept the faith.
“a better country, that is, an heavenly” (Heb 11:16) — what the Salzburgers were actually looking for.

pos: n. (the south-west German margravate, and the Swiss town whose 1526 disputation was the first great public debate between Rome and the Reformed)
etymology: From Old High German bad, a bath, for the hot springs; the name belongs to several places.
biblical_def: Baden is the name of the German margravate on the upper Rhine and of a Swiss town in Aargau, and both belong here. The disputation of Baden in Switzerland, in May and June 1526, was the first great set debate of the Reformation in the German-speaking lands: Johann Eck argued for the Roman side, Johannes Oecolampadius for the Reformed, Zwingli was refused a safe conduct and advised his colleague by letter, and the Catholic cantons declared Eck the winner and used the result against Zurich. The German margravate was divided in 1535 into Baden-Baden, which stayed Catholic, and Baden-Durlach, which became Lutheran and later had a Reformed ruler, so the two confessions faced each other across a single dynasty for two centuries. The dictionary records Baden for the disputation, because the public disputation on stated theses with an agreed rule of evidence is one of the Reformation's real contributions to the handling of controversy.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a disputation as a contest in words; a thesis as a position laid down; a margravate as the territory of a margrave; an umpire as one chosen to decide a dispute; and controversy as a dispute in writing.
webster_full: DISPUTATION, n. A contest in words; controversy in words; an exercise in colleges in which parties reason in opposition to each other.
THESIS, n. A position or proposition which a person advances and offers to maintain by argument.
MARGRAVATE, n. The territory or jurisdiction of a margrave, a title of nobility in Germany.
UMPIRE, n. A third person called in to decide a controversy or question submitted to arbitrators.
CONTROVERSY, n. Dispute; debate; agitation of contrary opinions; a dispute carried on in writing.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
For he mightily convinced the Jews, and that publickly, shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ.
corruption_summary: Swiss town of the 1526 disputation between Eck and Oecolampadius, and the German margravate divided in 1535 between a Catholic and a Lutheran line.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the public disputation itself: stated theses, named disputants, an agreed text as the rule, and a record. The Reformed cause lost the verdict at Baden, because the judges were the Catholic cantons, and gained the arguments, because they were published. The rule the Reformers insisted on is the one Isaiah lays down for any contest of this kind: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).

The second paragraph names the live temptation, which is to settle controversy by assertion or by crowd. Scripture commends the opposite. The Bereans tested a preacher against the text, and they “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11); Paul gives the two-stroke rule, “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21); and Luke describes Apollos at work in precisely the Baden manner, publicly and out of the text: he “mightily convinced the Jews, and that publickly, shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ” (Act 18:28). A disputation is a servant of the text or it is theatre.

“Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21) — the two-stroke rule of controversy.

pos: n. (the Lusatian city of Jacob Boehme the shoemaker, whose mystical writings shaped later German and English enthusiasm)
etymology: From a Slavic root gora, a hill, with a Germanised ending.
biblical_def: Gorlitz is a Lusatian city on the Neisse, Lutheran since 1525, a cloth town, and the place where Jacob Boehme kept a shoemaker's shop. Boehme, born in 1575 at Alt Seidenberg nearby, published Aurora in 1612 and was silenced by the town pastor Gregorius Richter; he wrote a great deal more before his death in 1624, and his works, printed abroad, shaped the German Pietists, the Philadelphians and the Behmenists in England, William Law, and through them a long line of later religious thought. Gorlitz also keeps a fifteenth-century replica of the Jerusalem Holy Sepulchre, built by a burgher who had made the pilgrimage. The dictionary records Boehme plainly and without the sneering that often attends him. He was a devout man who prayed and worked with his hands, and he taught a doctrine of God in which light and darkness are both eternal principles within the divine, which Scripture does not permit, and he taught it on the authority of what he had seen.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mystic as one who holds a pure and sublime devotion; a vision as something apparently seen otherwise than by ordinary sight; revelation as the act of disclosing what was secret; enthusiasm as a conceit of private revelation; and sufficiency as adequacy to the end proposed.
webster_full: MYSTIC, n. One of a sect of the Christian church, who profess to have direct intercourse with the Spirit of God.
VISION, n. Something imaginary; the act of seeing external objects; a supernatural appearance; a spectre.
REVELATION, n. The act of disclosing or discovering to others what was before unknown to them; that which is revealed, particularly the Scriptures.
ENTHUSIASM, n. A belief or conceit of private revelation; the vain confidence or opinion of a person that he has special divine communications.
SUFFICIENCY, n. The state of being adequate to the end proposed; qualification for any purpose; competence.
scriptures: This then is the message which we have heard of him, and declare unto you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.
Jas 1:17
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: Lusatian city of the shoemaker Jacob Boehme, whose visionary writings on light and darkness within God shaped later German and English enthusiasm.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is a doctrine of God drawn from a private vision, and in Boehme's case the specific error is the placing of a dark principle inside the divine nature. John forecloses it in the one sentence of Scripture that most directly addresses the question, and he presents it as the apostolic message rather than as an opinion: “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all” (1Jo 1:5). James says the same of God's action, that there is no alternation in him, “with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning” (Jas 1:17).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is the sufficiency of the written word against every claim of fresh sight. Isaiah supplies the test and applies it to men who claim to see: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). Paul states what the Scriptures are and what they are adequate for, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine” (2Ti 3:16). The dictionary does not doubt that Boehme experienced something. It denies that an experience is a source of doctrine, and notes that his readers for three centuries have taken the one thing from him he had no authority to give.

“with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning” (Jas 1:17) — no alternation in the divine nature.
“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the test applied to a man who claims to see.

pos: n. (the Upper Lusatian capital whose cathedral of Saint Peter has been shared by Catholic and Lutheran congregations since 1524, the oldest such arrangement in Germany)
etymology: From Upper Sorbian Budyšin, a Slavic settlement name, Germanised as Bautzen.
biblical_def: Bautzen is the capital of Upper Lusatia and the chief town of the Sorbs, the Slavic people of eastern Germany, whose language it still carries on its street signs. The Reformation came to the city in the fifteen-twenties, and in 1524 an arrangement was made for the collegiate church of Saint Peter which has lasted five hundred years: the chapter kept the choir for the Latin mass and the city took the nave for Lutheran preaching, with a barrier between them. It is the oldest simultaneum in Germany and the church is still shared. Bautzen also printed the first books in Upper Sorbian, and the Sorbian New Testament of 1706 by Michal Frencel was made there for a people of perhaps a hundred thousand. The dictionary records Bautzen for both facts and ranks the second higher. A shared building is a workable arrangement between confessions that cannot agree. A New Testament in the language of a small Slavic people is the thing the Reformation was for.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a nave as the body of a church; a choir as the part where the singers are placed; a partition as that which divides; a dialect as the form of a language in a province; and a version as a translation.
webster_full: NAVE, n. The middle or body of a church, extending from the balluster or railing of the door to the chief choir.
CHOIR, n. A collection of singers; the part of a church appropriated to the singers, separated from the chancel and nave.
PARTITION, n. That which divides or separates; a dividing wall; the act of dividing.
DIALECT, n. The form or idiom of a language peculiar to a province, or to a kingdom or state; the language of a province.
VERSION, n. A translation; the act of translating; the rendering of a work from one language into another.
scriptures: Act 2:8
And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?
So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
Rev 7:9

After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;
Eph 2:14
For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us;
corruption_summary: Upper Lusatian capital whose collegiate church has been shared by Catholic and Lutheran congregations since 1524, and where the Sorbian New Testament was printed in 1706.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the gospel belongs in small languages. The Sorbs numbered a hundred thousand or so and had no state, no court and no prospect; Bautzen printed their New Testament anyway. Pentecost settles the principle in the form of a question from the crowd: “And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?” (Act 2:8), and Paul makes intelligibility the test of any speech in the assembly, since otherwise “ye shall speak into the air” (1Co 14:9).

The second paragraph names the live temptation, which is to count languages worth translating by the size of the market. John's vision of the redeemed is counted the other way, “a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Rev 7:9). As to the barrier in the middle of Saint Peter's, the dictionary allows it as a civil arrangement and will not call it unity, because what Christ is said to have done is the opposite of building one: he “hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us” (Eph 2:14). A shared roof is peaceable. It is not the same thing as one body.

pos: n. (the Silesian town of the prince-bishops of Breslau, from which the Catholic Reformation was pressed on a largely Lutheran duchy)
etymology: From the river Neisse, a Slavic hydronym; the Polish form is Nysa.
biblical_def: Neisse in Silesia was the chief town of the duchy held by the prince-bishops of Breslau and so a Catholic island in a province that had gone overwhelmingly Lutheran in the fifteen-twenties. From the later sixteenth century it was the base of the Catholic recovery in Silesia: a Jesuit college was founded in 1622, and after the Habsburg victory over the Bohemian Protestants the churches of the duchy and of the crown lands were taken back, Lutheran ministers expelled, and conformity pressed by commissions, with the Peace of Westphalia securing only three plain timber churches of peace for the whole province. Frederick the Great's conquest of Silesia in 1740 reversed the position again. The dictionary records Neisse because Silesia is the best-documented example of a province changed by administration twice within a century, and because the churches of peace, built of wood outside the walls and holding thousands, are the plainest monument in Europe to a people who would not stop assembling.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conformity as compliance with an established form; a commission as a body of persons authorised to act; an assembly as a company met together; timber as wood for building; and constancy as firmness of mind.
webster_full: CONFORMITY, n. Correspondence with a model or pattern; compliance with the usages of the established church.
COMMISSION, n. A number of persons joined in an office or trust; the warrant by which authority is conferred.
ASSEMBLY, n. A company of persons collected together in one place, usually for some common purpose.
TIMBER, n. That sort of wood which is proper for buildings or for tools, utensils, furniture and the like.
CONSTANCY, n. Fixedness; firmness of mind; steadiness; perseverance in a purpose or opinion.
scriptures: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
Act 2:46
And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart,
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
Act 5:42
And daily in the temple, and in every house, they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ.
corruption_summary: Silesian town of the prince-bishops of Breslau, base of the Catholic recovery that took back the province's churches and left Protestants three timber churches of peace.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the use of commissions, registers and the confiscation of buildings to reverse a people's religion, which Silesia suffered twice. The dictionary notes what the Silesian Lutherans did when their churches were taken, which was to go on meeting: at the border, in the woods, and finally in three enormous timber barns built outside town walls by permission of a treaty. The command they were obeying is explicit and is given against a known tendency: “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is” (Heb 10:25).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that the church is a gathering and not a building. Christ fixes the minimum and attaches himself to it, “For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Mat 18:20); the first church met in both large and small places, “daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house” (Act 2:46); and when forbidden the apostles simply continued, for “daily in the temple, and in every house, they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ” (Act 5:42). Taking a congregation's roof is a serious injury and it is not a solution.
